questions.q: What does RPO (Recovery Point Objective) actually measure?
options: The maximum acceptable data loss, measured as time since the last good copy
The maximum acceptable time a system can remain down
The number of Availability Zones a workload is deployed across
The total cost of running a DR environment
questions.explain: RPO answers how much data the business can afford to lose, measured as time since the last good copy — a completely different question from how long recovery itself takes.

questions.q: A workload has an RPO of 1 hour. Which backup or replication approach does this lesson say would actually meet that target?
options: A nightly backup job, since 24 hours is close enough to 1 hour
No backup strategy at all, since RPO only applies to RTO decisions
Incremental backups or log shipping on an hourly cadence
A cold, restore-from-scratch rebuild using Infrastructure as Code
questions.explain: An RPO of 1 hour requires backups or replication at least that frequent — nightly backups would allow up to 24 hours of data loss, which fails a 1-hour RPO target.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what decision does RTO primarily drive?
options: Which Availability Zones a workload is deployed into
How much standby capacity must already exist and be ready to take traffic versus how much can be rebuilt after the disaster is declared
How often tagging policies are audited
The naming convention used for backup files
questions.explain: RTO drives standby capacity decisions: a tight RTO requires a warm or hot standby already provisioned, while a loose RTO allows infrastructure to be rebuilt from Infrastructure as Code and data restored from backup after the fact.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say a business should set RTO and RPO per workload tier rather than as one blanket policy?
options: Because cloud providers require different targets for different services
Because tighter RTO/RPO targets cost more, and applying the strictest targets to every workload spends money protecting against a cost the business never actually quantified for that workload
Because RTO and RPO cannot legally differ between systems in the same company
Because only financial systems are allowed to have an RPO at all
questions.explain: Tighter targets always cost more in standing infrastructure, replication tooling, and operational complexity, so applying the tightest targets uniformly — e.g. to an internal wiki as well as a payments ledger — wastes money the business never actually decided to spend.

questions.q: What is the key difference between a warm standby and a hot standby, as described in this lesson?
options: A warm standby is located in the same Availability Zone as production; a hot standby is in a different zone
There is no real difference — the terms are interchangeable
A hot standby only applies to RPO decisions, never to RTO
A warm standby runs at reduced capacity and is scaled up on failover; a hot standby already runs at full production capacity, ready to take traffic immediately
questions.explain: A warm standby exists in the DR region at reduced capacity and scales up only when failover is declared, while a hot standby is already running at full capacity, which is what lets it meet an RTO measured in seconds to minutes.
